items.title: Morning Briefing: Nov. 7, 2026
items.excerpt: Here's a rundown of all the news you need to know for Saturday, including Russian President Vladimir Putin confirming that the next round of Russia-US-Ukraine talks will begin Tuesday in Abu Dhabi; US President Donald Trump naming Stephen Miller as White House chief of staff to replace Susie Wiles and saying he plans Cabinet changes after the midterm election losses; and bomb threats targeting flights, airports and media outlets in at least five European countries. Russian President Vladimir Putin confirmed that the next round of talks between Russia, the US and Ukraine is expected to begin next Tuesday in Abu Dhabi, with Russian state media reporting the talks would last two days. Putin said he invited members of the Russian delegation, headed by presidential aide Vladimir Medinsky, to a UN Security Council meeting ahead of the negotiations, Tass reported. US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff previously said the parties intend to discuss security guarantees, de-escalation, humanitarian issues and further steps toward a peaceful settlement. - Trump names Stephen Miller chief of staff, says he plans Cabinet changes after midterm losses Trump announced that Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller will replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff starting Monday, while Wiles moves to the Trump political operation. “Sometimes in life, you have to make moves,” Trump told reporters, saying he “wanted to make a change.” Trump said he plans to make changes to his Cabinet after Republicans lost both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections earlier this week, telling CBS News’ 60 Minutes, “I do, yeah. Little bit,” when asked whether he plans to fire anyone, in an interview set to air Sunday. - Bomb threats target flights, media outlets in at least 5 European countries Bomb threats targeted flights, airports and media organizations in at least five European countries, prompting security inspections and evacuations, according to authorities and the media. Two aircraft departing from London and Brussels were diverted to Sofia and landed safely, while Czech police inspected nine aircraft following anonymous threats against four arrivals and five departures at Prague Airport. The French prime minister’s office said four aircraft flying over French territory received threats and all landed safely, and Copenhagen Police completed security checks at the city’s airport. Several Irish media organizations, including RTE, evacuated their premises after a threatening email was sent to broadcasters and news outlets in Ireland and Britain, with Irish Taoiseach Micheal Martin calling the threats “worrying.” The incidents followed similar threats Thursday against at least 18 flights across Europe.

items.title: Daly Says Fed May Need More Rate Increases as Inflation Persists | EconoTimes
items.excerpt: By Miriam Hart Nov 7, 2026, 9:43 AM UTC ... U.S. wage growth remained below the latest annual inflation reading, and San Francisco Federal Reserve Bank President Mary Daly said the Fed may need to raise rates again as price pressures persist. Daly made the assessment in a Nov. 6 interview with CNBC. She said officials would consider incoming economic information before deciding whether or when to act. “My expectation is we’re going to have to tighten policy further,” she said. Daly did not set a timetable or specify the size of a possible increase. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that employers added 165,000 jobs in October and unemployment edged down to 4.1%. Average hourly earnings rose 3.1% from a year earlier that month, while the consumer price index increased 3.7% year over year in September. Daly welcomed the job gains but said inflation continued to weigh on household finances. She said people were still finding work and spending, while pay gains failed to keep pace with prices. She described labor conditions as steady but not unusually strong, and said inflation’s persistence concerned her more than economic growth. Daly also said inflation had remained high for almost six years, with its burden spreading across households. The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) raised its target range for the federal funds rate by 0.25 percentage point in September, to 3.75% to 4%. On Oct. 28, it left the range unchanged and said additional information would guide its policy stance. Daly said she supported both decisions and continued to favor a gradual approach. Richmond Fed President Thomas Barkin also expects further increases may be needed, CNBC reported, though he has not identified when. The next report on October CPI is scheduled for Nov. 10, and the FOMC’s next meeting is set for Dec. 8-9.

items.excerpt: NEW YORK: The US dollar index jumped on Friday and was on pace for its biggest daily percentage gain in seven weeks as it extended gains after a stronger-than-expected US payrolls report. The Labor Department said US nonfarm payrolls jumped by 165,000 jobs last month, topping the 65,000 estimate of economists polled by Reuters, after an upwardly revised 60,000 gain in September, while the unemployment rate dipped to 4.1 percent. The report gives the Federal Reserve latitude to continue to hike interest rates, and market expectations for an increase of at least 25 basis points at the central bank’s December meeting moved back up towards 80 percent in the wake of the report, according to the CME FedWatch Tool. ... New York Federal Reserve President John Williams said on Friday that US economic growth has remained remarkably resilient in the face of successive shocks but inflation is too high and it is essential to bring it back to 2 percent.

items.title: Fed’s Williams says energy prices have already peaked despite new Iran fighting | Hellenic Shipping News Worldwide
items.excerpt: Federal Reserve Bank of New York President John Williams said today he does not expect a sustained rise in energy prices for the rest of the year, despite renewed conflict in the Middle East. Williams told a conference at his bank that market expectations for oil prices to decline over the next six to 12 months remain reasonable. He said the fundamentals suggest energy prices are likely around their peak and should come down over time. The Fed official said inflation remains “far too high” and that monetary policy is focused on how energy prices impact inflation. Williams added that artificial intelligence investment is currently driving inflation, though he expects AI to become a positive supply shock in the longer term. His base case sees broader AI use boosting productivity. Williams said the Fed is actively debating scenarios around inflation and remains committed to bringing inflation back to 2%. He stressed the importance of looking at underlying inflation factors rather than just specific measures, noting that government technical changes could better reconcile differences between PCE inflation and CPI.

items.title: Live updates: Trump taps Stephen Miller as new chief of staff
items.excerpt: November 07, 2026, 2:14 PM EST By NBC News ## What to know today - WILES OUT: President Donald Trump announced Friday that White House chief of staff Susie Wiles would be leaving her role this week and would be replaced by deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller. - STILL COUNTING: Votes are still being counted in the shockingly close Alaska and Mississippi Senate races. Democratic candidates Mary Peltola and Scott Colom continue to narrowly lead their Republican opponents, GOP Sens. Dan Sullivan and Cindy Hyde-Smith, respectively. - CALIFORNIA BALLOTS: The Justice Department moved to dismiss its bid to separate more than 20,000 California ballots it alleged were cast by noncitizens. California officials had argued that the list was out of date and included legitimate voters. ## Trump accuses Democrats of 'criminal extortion' In a Truth Social post, Trump said he is ordering the Justice Department to investigate what he calls “criminal extortion” by Democratic leaders, accusing them of threatening administration officials with impeachment and Republican donors with imprisonment. Trump also singled out Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., accusing her of targeting young Republican supporters. “The imprisonment should be against these EXTORTIONISTS,” Trump wrote, adding: “By copy of this statement, I am ordering the Department of Justice to look into this criminal act, immediately!” The president appeared to be responding to posts by some Democratic lawmakers calling for investigations into the Trump administration in the wake of widespread wins for their party on Tuesday. Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., wrote on X on Tuesday, “Lawyer up.” In response to the president’s post today, Slotkin wrote in a post on X, “This shouldn’t be controversial: if you break the law or use taxpayer dollars to enrich yourself, you should be held accountable. If you didn’t break the law, then it’s all good.” ## Trump says he offered UFC's Dana White a job as press secretary In a post on Truth Social, the president said he offered Dana White, the president and CEO of the Ultimate Fighting Championship, a job as White House press secretary. "I am pleased to announce that the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior, has been offered the job of Press Secretary of the United States," the president wrote, adding later: "Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other. Dana, please take the job!" ... ## Trump floats being kind to Democrats in exchange for bipartisan deals In a new clip released ahead of his full "60 Minutes" interview airing Sunday, Trump said he could go six months without insulting Democrats if it meant getting a deal done. Asked by CBS News' Ross Douthat about newly elected Texas Democratic Sen. James Talarico expressing interest in working with him on immigration, Trump noted that other Democrats had also expressed a willingness to cooperate. Trump acknowledged calling Talarico “Talafreako” during the campaign as well as referring to many Democrats as “Dumbocrats.” Brendan Smialowski / AFP / Getty On whether he could refrain from insults for six months to secure a deal, Trump responded, “Very easily.” The president's comments come days after Democrats flipped the House and Senate in the midterm elections, with NBC News projecting Democrats could have 259 House seats next year, far beyond the 218 needed for a majority. In the Senate, Democratic candidates also flipped Senate seats in South Carolina, Texas, Maine and Ohio, cementing a Democratic majority in Congress' upper chamber.

Democrats are also promising early votes on legislation to stop the war with Iran and to reverse some of President Donald Trump’s trade tariffs. Ron DeSantis, the Florida governor, calls it an “extinction-level event” for the party. Ted Cruz, the Texas senator, compares it to a “Watergate-level repudiation.” The party is divided on how to move forward. Some want to return to fiscal conservatism. Others suggest embracing President Donald Trump’s politics. Trump's role in shaping the party's future is a key question. GOP infighting is expected to intensify, with leadership battles and policy decisions looming. The party must also address its appeal to younger voters and minorities to regain lost ground. Young voters overwhelmingly backed Democrats this year. The question is whether they'll stay WASHINGTON (AP) — Young voters voted overwhelmingly for Democrats in the midterm elections, driven by economic concerns and disillusionment with President Donald Trump’s war in Iran. Also motivating some young voters was the rise of artificial intelligence and the data centers powering the technology. The AP Voter Poll shows about 7 in 10 voters under 30 supported Democrats in local congressional races. That was a dramatic shift from 2024. Experts say many young voters aren't firmly aligned with either party and are influenced by current economic conditions. Their dissatisfaction with Republican leadership is clear, but this support could shift if Democrats fail to address key issues.
